implementation_notes: The injector is the Spring ApplicationContext (or any JSR-330 injector): components declare dependencies through an annotated constructor, field or setter, and the container resolves the graph from component scanning or @Configuration classes while applying singleton/prototype/request scopes. What replaces the hand-written assembler is annotation-driven binding; constructor injection is recommended because it makes components immutable and fully initialised, with setter injection kept for optional dependencies and JMX-style reconfiguration. A plain composition root with new calls remains the dependency-free alternative.
pitfalls: Constructor ambiguity: with several constructors only one may be @Autowired(required=true) - otherwise the container's resolution rules pick for you.
Circular constructor dependencies abort start-up; break them by injecting Provider<T> or by restructuring.
Scope mismatches (a singleton holding a request/session bean) pin short-lived state - keep constructor injection and check scopes.

variants.name: Spring / JSR-330 annotation-driven container

variants.name: Jakarta CDI container
variants.idiom_name: @Inject injection points + @Produces factories with qualifiers and scopes
variants.implementation_notes: Jakarta CDI standardises the same idea across Jakarta EE runtimes and CDI-aware frameworks (Quarkus, Helidon, Weld): @Inject selects an injection point, @Produces declares factory methods, @Qualifier/@Named disambiguate competing implementations, and built-in scopes (@ApplicationScoped, @RequestScoped) carry lifetimes. The provider lives in the runtime, so the application code is portable between compliant containers and needs no extra dependency. Constructor injection remains the recommended consumer side; field injection is legal but hides the dependency.
pitfalls: In a slim container without bean discovery, an unannotated class is silently not injectable.
Producer methods need matching qualifiers: two candidates for one injection point fail deployment or resolve ambiguously.

variants.name: Hand-wired composition root without a container
variants.idiom_name: plain constructors and factory methods assembled in main
variants.implementation_notes: Java needs no framework for dependency injection: have every class take its collaborators as constructor parameters of interface types and assemble the graph in main or a dedicated factory class, holding long-lived instances in fields. This keeps the classpath free of container dependencies and the graph readable in one file, which is often right for libraries, tests and small services; move to a container when lifecycle management, proxying or a large graph makes hand wiring expensive.
pitfalls: Hand-rolled singletons creep in (static INSTANCE/getInstance) - keep instances in the root instead.
Interfaces must be owned by the consumer's module, or the dependency arrow flips back to the implementation.
